title: United States | Consumer Compliance for Banks (UDAAP, Reg E, Reg Z, ECOA, Privacy)
tagline: Run consumer compliance the way US examiners expect: CMS and training, UDAAP, Reg E disputes, Reg Z and loan originators, ECOA, complaints and privacy.
description:
This quest teaches the **US federal consumer protection rules** that bank staff apply every day, built on the CFPB's Supervision and Examination Manual (compliance management review and UDAAP procedures), Regulation E (12 CFR Part 1005), Regulation Z (12 CFR Part 1026), Regulation B (12 CFR Part 1002, including the April 2026 amendment effective 21 July 2026), Regulation P (12 CFR Part 1016) and Regulation F (12 CFR Part 1006), and the OCC's compliance management handbook.

You will learn how a consumer compliance management system works and why training is one of its parts, the three UDAAP tests, Regulation E error resolution timelines, Truth in Lending mortgage disclosure timing, the loan originator screening and periodic training duty in 12 CFR 1026.36(f)(3), equal credit and adverse action rules, complaint handling, privacy notices and opt-outs, and where debt collection rules reach a bank.

It is meant for staff of US banks in consumer-facing, product, marketing, lending, disputes, complaints and compliance roles. Examiners expect role-specific, up-to-date consumer compliance training, and loan originator employees must receive periodic training under Regulation Z. This quest builds knowledge and does not replace your bank's own policies and procedures.
audience: Branch, call centre and digital banking staff at US banks who serve consumers
Product, marketing and sales managers who design or promote consumer products
Mortgage and consumer lending staff, including registered loan originators
Card disputes, deposit operations, collections and complaints teams
Compliance officers, auditors and managers who oversee the consumer compliance programme
outcomes: Describe the parts of a consumer compliance management system and what examiners expect from training
Apply the unfair, deceptive and abusive tests to products, ads and scripts
Resolve electronic fund transfer errors within Regulation E's timelines
Apply Regulation Z mortgage disclosure timing and the loan originator screening and training rule
Identify prohibited bases, discouragement and adverse action duties under ECOA and Regulation B, including the 2026 change
Handle complaints, privacy notices and opt-outs, and collections risks in a way that stands up to examination

quest.name: The Consumer Exam
quest.premise: You have just joined the compliance team of Prairie Lantern Bank, N.A., a fictional national bank with USD 14 billion in assets, headquartered in Kansas City with operations in Denver, Phoenix and Atlanta. The CFPB has announced a consumer compliance examination. Chief Compliance Officer Maya Okafor wants you ready: with disputes lead Luis Herrera, mortgage manager Grace Liu, product head Tom Brennan and complaints lead Aisha Rahman, clear five stages and then face the examiner's questions.

sessions.title: The Consumer Compliance Management System and Why Training Matters
sessions.summary: Meet the US consumer regulators, learn the parts of a compliance management system the CFPB examines, and see why role-based, timely training is one of them.
objectives: Explain which agency supervises a US bank for federal consumer financial law and why size matters
Describe the two components and four programme parts of a compliance management system
State what examiners expect from compliance training, including timing, tailoring and records
Link sales incentives to training on consent, accurate terms and reporting misconduct

cards.title: Day one: the consumer exam letter
cards.setting: Compliance floor, Prairie Lantern Bank head office, Kansas City, Missouri. 8:30 am.

lines.text: Your badge opens the compliance floor. On your desk sits a printed letter and a sticky note: 'Read this first. Maya.'
Welcome. I'm Maya Okafor, Chief Compliance Officer. That letter says the CFPB will examine our consumer compliance management system next quarter.
Tom Brennan, product and marketing. I'm launching a new rewards checking account in six weeks. Please tell me the exam won't stall it.
Luis Herrera, deposit operations. I run the card disputes team in Denver. Examiners always ask for our dispute files.
Aisha Rahman, complaints. And they always ask what our complaints are telling us, and what we did about it.
Grace Liu, mortgage lending in Phoenix. My loan officers have their own training rule, so count me in.
Five stages, then the examiner's questions. Stage one: who supervises us, what a compliance management system is, and why training sits inside it.

cards.title: US consumer protection in five scenes

scenes.heading: The laws
scenes.narration: Congress wrote the consumer financial laws: Truth in Lending, Electronic Fund Transfer, Equal Credit Opportunity, Gramm-Leach-Bliley privacy and others. The Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 added a ban on unfair, deceptive or abusive acts or practices, known as UDAAP.

scenes.heading: The CFPB writes most rules
scenes.narration: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau issues the main implementing rules, such as Regulation B for equal credit, E for electronic transfers, P for privacy and Z for truth in lending.

scenes.heading: Who examines a bank
scenes.narration: Banks with more than 10 billion US dollars in assets are supervised by the CFPB for federal consumer financial law. Their prudential regulator, the OCC, the Federal Reserve or the FDIC, examines the rest, and examines smaller banks for consumer law too.

scenes.heading: The compliance management system
scenes.narration: Examiners do not only hunt for violations. They judge the system a bank uses to prevent, find and fix them: its compliance management system, or CMS.

scenes.heading: Training is part of the system
scenes.narration: Training is one of the named parts of a compliance programme. If staff do not know the rules, policies alone will not protect customers.

cards.title: The CMS the CFPB examines
cards.caption: The CFPB manual describes two linked components: oversight by the board and management, and a compliance programme with four parts.

items.label: Board and management oversight
items.detail: Sets the tone, approves policy, funds compliance, manages change and holds people accountable.

items.label: Policies and procedures
items.detail: Written, current, cover each product's full life cycle and match board-approved policy.

items.label: Training
items.detail: Tailored to each role, updated before new products or rule changes, consistent with policy.

items.label: Monitoring and audit
items.detail: Monitoring finds weaknesses early; audit tests the whole system independently.

items.label: Consumer complaint response
items.detail: Records, investigates, escalates and learns from every complaint.

cards.question: A bank uses an outside firm to run its card dispute call centre. What does the CFPB compliance management manual say about responsibility for consumer law compliance?
options: It passes to the service provider under the contract
The bank keeps it, and must oversee the provider
It is shared equally between the bank and the provider
It applies only if the provider is also a bank
cards.explanation: The manual is clear that a bank may outsource operations but cannot outsource responsibility for complying with federal consumer financial law. It must oversee the provider, including its training.

cards.title: What examiners look for in training
cards.body:
The CFPB's compliance management review module lists what good training looks like. In our own words:

- **Tailored**: specific to the job, including product development, marketing and customer service, not one generic course for everyone.
- **Timely**: updated **before** a new or changed product launches and before a new or changed rule takes effect.
- **Consistent**: it reinforces the bank's written policies and procedures.
- **Deep enough for specialists**: compliance staff get the training they need to run the programme.

The manual says fair lending and UDAAP requirements belong in training for all relevant officers and staff, **including audit personnel**. Board members need enough information to understand the bank's duties and the resources they require.

Examiners then rate the training programme on a five-point scale from strong to critically deficient.

cards.title: How an examiner tests your training

items.label: Schedules and completion records
items.detail: For board, senior management, compliance staff, managers and front-line staff.

items.label: Compliance officer's role
items.detail: Who chose, reviewed or delivered the content.

items.label: Sample the materials
items.detail: Fair lending, new rules, new products and channels, marketing scripts.

items.label: Fixes from findings
items.detail: Training built after audit, exam or complaint findings.

items.label: Sales practices content
items.detail: Ethics, reporting concerns, describing terms, evidence of consent.

items.label: Late completers and plans
items.detail: Follow-up on missed deadlines and the next 12 months' plan.

cards.title: Match the CMS part to what it does
cards.prompt: Link each part of the compliance management system to its job.

pairs.right: Approves compliance policy, provides resources and acts on compliance reports
Turns legal requirements into day-to-day steps for each product
Makes sure each person knows the rules that apply to their own role
Frequent, less formal checks, often by the business, to catch problems early
Less frequent, formal and independent testing of the whole system
Resolves each complaint and spots patterns that signal harm

cards.title: The rewards account
cards.setting: Product team room, Kansas City. 2:15 pm.

lines.text: Here's the plan: a rewards checking account with a sign-up bonus. Branch staff get a small bonus for each one they open.
Incentives aren't banned. But examiners ask for compensation plans and look hard at sales goals.
Training is set for launch week. A short video about the features.
Launch week is too late, and features aren't enough. The manual expects training before rollout and content on consent and describing terms accurately.
And if customers start complaining about accounts they never asked for, I need to know how to escalate it.

cards.title: Training for the rewards launch
cards.situation: Tom wants to launch the rewards checking account in six weeks. Branch staff will earn a per-account incentive. The current plan is a 10-minute product video in launch week. Maya asks you to recommend a training approach she can defend to CFPB examiners.

choices.text: Build role-based training before launch: product terms, how to describe conditions accurately, getting and recording customer consent, how to raise concerns, and track completion
choices.outcome: Best. This matches what the manual expects for new products and sales incentives: timely, role-specific training on accurate descriptions, consent evidence and reporting misconduct, with completion records examiners can review.

choices.text: Keep the launch-week video but add a slide reminding staff to be honest
choices.outcome: Partly right. A reminder is better than nothing, but it arrives late and does not teach consent, accurate terms or how to report problems, and it gives examiners little evidence.

choices.text: Skip extra training because staff already did annual compliance training
choices.outcome: Poor. Annual generic training does not cover a new product with sales incentives. Examiners expect training updated in advance of new or changed products.

choices.text: Delay training until complaints show whether there is a problem
choices.outcome: Poor. Waiting for harm is the opposite of what a CMS is for. Complaints should trigger more training, not replace it.

cards.title: Real case: Wells Fargo sales practices, 2016
cards.body:
In September 2016 the CFPB fined **Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.** USD 100 million over the secret opening of deposit and credit card accounts that customers had not authorised.

According to the CFPB, staff were pushed by **sales targets and incentive pay**. They opened accounts and moved customers' money into them without consent, which often caused fees. The bank's own analysis found more than **2 million** accounts that may not have been authorised.

The bank also paid USD 35 million to the OCC and USD 50 million to the City and County of Los Angeles, and had to refund victims.

**Why it matters for training:** this case is why the CFPB manual now asks for training on sales practices, consent evidence, accurate descriptions of products and how staff report misconduct. Incentives that reward volume need controls and training that reward doing it right.

Source: CFPB enforcement action page, docket 2016-CFPB-0015.

cards.title: Real case: Bank of America card accounts, 2023
cards.body:
In July 2023 the CFPB ordered **Bank of America, N.A.** to pay a USD 30 million civil money penalty and redress customers.

The CFPB found that in some cases the bank had **opened credit card accounts without customer consent**, pulling credit reports without a permissible purpose. It also found **deceptive** marketing: a sign-up bonus advertised online as if open to all, then refused to people who applied by phone or in a branch, and bonuses promised but not paid because of **employee error**.

The findings touched three laws at once: Truth in Lending (Regulation Z), the Fair Credit Reporting Act and the Consumer Financial Protection Act's UDAAP ban.

**Lesson:** staff who sell a product need to know its real terms in every channel, and how to record consent. Training gaps show up as 'employee error' in an enforcement order.

Source: CFPB enforcement action page, docket 2023-CFPB-0007.

cards.back: Compliance management system: how a bank sets, communicates, builds in, checks and corrects its consumer compliance duties.
Unfair, deceptive or abusive acts or practices, banned by the Dodd-Frank Act for providers of consumer financial products and their service providers.
The OCC, Federal Reserve or FDIC: the agency that supervises a bank for safety and soundness, depending on its charter.
The bank must make sure vendors who touch consumers follow the law and are trained. Responsibility stays with the bank.
How the bank updates policies, systems and training before a new product or a new rule goes live.
Examiners rate each CMS part from strong or satisfactory down to deficient, seriously deficient or critically deficient.

cards.question: A new Regulation Z amendment takes effect in three months. When does the CFPB manual expect the bank's training to be updated?
options: Within a year after the effective date
Only after examiners find a violation
In advance of the effective date
At the next annual training cycle
cards.explanation: The manual expects the training programme to be updated proactively, before new or changed rules take effect and before new or changed products roll out, so staff know their duties on day one.

cards.title: Make your training records exam-ready
Stage one take-aways
items: The CFPB supervises banks above USD 10 billion in assets for federal consumer financial law; the OCC, Fed or FDIC covers the rest.
A CMS has board and management oversight plus a compliance programme: policies, training, monitoring and audit, and complaint response.
Training must be role-specific, consistent with policy and updated before new products and rule changes.
A bank can outsource tasks but never responsibility; vendors with consumer contact must be trained and overseen.
Sales incentives need training on accurate descriptions, consent and reporting misconduct, as the Wells Fargo case shows.

cards.prompt: Think about the last product or rule change in your area. When did you receive training about it: before, on, or after the day it went live? What would you change?

quiz.question: Which agency supervises a US bank with USD 25 billion in assets for compliance with federal consumer financial law?
options: FinCEN
The CFPB
The FFIEC
OFAC
quiz.explanation: Banks with more than USD 10 billion in assets are supervised by the CFPB for federal consumer financial law. FinCEN covers the Bank Secrecy Act, OFAC sanctions, and the FFIEC is an interagency council.

quiz.question: In the CFPB's model of a compliance management system, which two components work together?
options: Internal audit, and external review by the bank's examiners
Product design approval, and marketing sign-off by the legal team
Risk appetite setting, and capital and liquidity planning
Board and management oversight, and the compliance programme
quiz.explanation: The CFPB manual describes two interdependent components: board and management oversight, and a compliance programme made up of policies and procedures, training, monitoring and/or audit, and complaint response.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four parts of the compliance programme in the CFPB manual?
options: Capital adequacy planning
Training
Consumer complaint response
Monitoring and/or audit
quiz.explanation: The four parts are policies and procedures, training, monitoring and/or audit, and consumer complaint response. Capital planning is a prudential topic, not part of the consumer CMS programme.

quiz.question: A bank plans to launch a new overdraft feature next month. Branch staff will get training two weeks after launch. What is the main weakness an examiner would note?
options: Branch staff should never be trained on overdraft
Training is only required for the compliance team
Training should be updated before the product rolls out
New products need no training if the disclosures are correct
quiz.explanation: The manual expects training to be updated in advance of new or changed products. Correct disclosures do not replace staff knowing how to describe and sell the product.

quiz.question: The CFPB manual says fair lending and UDAAP requirements should be part of training for relevant staff. Which group does it expressly include that banks often forget?
options: Only senior executives
Only external lawyers
Audit personnel
Only call centre agents
quiz.explanation: The manual says these requirements should be built into training for all relevant officers and employees, including audit personnel, so that auditors can recognise problems.

quiz.question: A card servicing vendor handles customer calls for your bank. What should the bank be able to show examiners about the vendor's staff?
options: That they are appropriately trained for their consumer contact
That each agent holds an individual licence issued by the CFPB
That the vendor has agreed to accept all legal liability instead
That the vendor's staff never discuss fees or terms with customers
quiz.explanation: Examiners request documents showing that service providers with consumer contact or compliance duties are appropriately trained. The bank keeps legal responsibility.

quiz.question: Which item would a CFPB examiner most likely request when reviewing training related to sales practices?
options: The bank's dividend policy and capital distribution plans
Branch opening hours and staffing rotas for the quarter
Records of staff holidays and leave approvals for each business unit
Content on getting and keeping evidence of customer consent
quiz.explanation: The manual asks examiners to check training on sales practices, including standards of ethical behaviour, reporting concerns, describing terms accurately and evidence of consumer consent for product openings and upselling.

quiz.question: According to the CFPB, what did Wells Fargo employees do in the 2016 sales practices case?
options: Refused to open accounts for applicants from minority areas
Opened accounts without customers' knowledge or consent
Failed to file currency transaction reports for cash deposits
Charged card interest above state usury caps for years
quiz.explanation: The CFPB found that employees, spurred by sales targets and incentives, secretly opened deposit and credit card accounts and moved money into them without consent.

quiz.question: Monitoring and audit both test compliance. Which statement matches the CFPB manual?
options: Monitoring is more frequent and informal; audit is formal and independent
Monitoring must be carried out by external firms, never the business
Audit happens daily, while monitoring takes place every three years
They are the same activity, so examiners do not need to distinguish between them
quiz.explanation: The manual says monitoring is generally more frequent and less formal and may be done by the business unit, while audit is less frequent, more formal and requires independence.

quiz.question: Units at your bank keep missing training deadlines. What will a CFPB examiner look for?
options: Proof that the training deadlines were removed or relaxed
A waiver signed by each employee who missed the deadline
Records of follow-up, escalation and enforcement for those units
Evidence that the training was made optional for the busiest units
quiz.explanation: The manual directs examiners to review records of follow-up, escalation and enforcement for units whose completion rates miss the bank's standards or deadlines.

sessions.title: UDAAP: Unfair, Deceptive and Abusive Acts or Practices
sessions.summary: Learn the three UDAAP tests from the CFPB examination procedures, how examiners judge ads and scripts, and what real enforcement cases teach front-line and product staff.
objectives: Apply the three-part tests for unfair and deceptive practices and the two-limb abusive standard
Judge marketing by net impression, target audience and the four Ps
Explain why technical compliance with a specific rule does not prevent a UDAAP finding
Use complaints, refunds and chargebacks as early warning signals

lines.text: Look at this billboard: 'Free checking. Earn USD 300.' Clean, bold, done.
Free if what? And USD 300 if what?
The conditions are on the website. Direct deposit, minimum balance, 90 days. Standard stuff.
My team already gets calls from people who thought 'free' meant no monthly fee at all. They're upset when it appears.
A rule-compliant ad can still be deceptive. Today you learn the three UDAAP tests examiners use.
Three tests? I thought deceptive was just lying.

cards.title: Unfair, deceptive, abusive: three separate tests

scenes.heading: One ban, three standards
scenes.narration: The Dodd-Frank Act makes it unlawful for any provider of consumer financial products, or its service provider, to engage in unfair, deceptive or abusive acts or practices. Each word has its own legal test.

scenes.heading: Unfair
scenes.narration: A practice is unfair when it causes or is likely to cause substantial injury, consumers cannot reasonably avoid that injury, and the injury is not outweighed by benefits to consumers or competition.

scenes.heading: Deceptive
scenes.narration: A practice is deceptive when it misleads or is likely to mislead, the consumer's reading is reasonable, and the point is material, meaning it would affect their choice or conduct.

scenes.heading: Abusive
scenes.narration: A practice is abusive when it materially interferes with a consumer's ability to understand a term, or takes unreasonable advantage of their lack of understanding, inability to protect themselves, or reasonable reliance on the provider.

scenes.heading: Complaints are clues
scenes.narration: Examiners read complaints closely. Many similar complaints about the same product are a red flag, and even one serious complaint can trigger a review.

cards.title: Unfair vs deceptive at a glance

items.label: Core question
items.left: Does it cause harm consumers can't avoid?
items.right: Does it mislead a reasonable consumer?

items.label: Element one
items.right: A representation, omission or practice likely to mislead

items.label: Element two
items.right: Reasonable interpretation by the target audience

items.label: Typical example
items.left: Repeat fees on the same returned item
items.right: Headline claim contradicted by hidden conditions

cards.question: Under the unfairness test, which of these is usually enough to count as substantial injury?
options: A small fee charged to a very large number of people
A customer's mild annoyance at a long queue
A purely speculative risk with no evidence
A consumer choosing a product they later regret
cards.explanation: The CFPB's UDAAP procedures note that a small harm to many people can be substantial injury, and that monetary harm such as fees is typical. Trivial or speculative harms usually are not enough.

cards.title: How examiners judge 'deceptive'
cards.body:
The CFPB procedures give practical tests for deception:

- **Net impression.** A statement is judged in the context of the whole ad or conversation, not word by word.
- **Fine print does not always cure.** A small-print or later disclosure may not fix a misleading headline or a prominent claim.
- **Target audience.** If you market to older customers, students or people in financial distress, ask how a reasonable member of *that group* would understand it.
- **A significant minority is enough.** If a meaningful share of the audience is misled, the claim can be deceptive even if most people understand it.
- **Materiality.** Information about cost, benefits and restrictions is presumed material.

The FTC's **four Ps** help: is the disclosure **prominent**, is it **presented** clearly, is it **placed** where people look, and is it in **proximity** to the claim it qualifies?

Puffery, obvious exaggeration nobody takes literally, is not deceptive.

cards.title: Unfair, deceptive or abusive?
cards.prompt: Put each practice in the UDAAP category it most clearly fits.

items.text: Charging a second NSF fee each time a merchant re-presents the same returned item
Advertising 'no fees' when a monthly fee applies below a balance most customers hold
Freezing accounts on a fraud flag without review when lesser steps were available
Burying a key condition so consumers cannot understand how the product works
Promising a bonus to all applicants and refusing it to those who apply in branch
Steering a confused older customer into a costly add-on they clearly don't grasp
Showing a low monthly payment while hiding a large balloon payment

lines.text: Legal says the billboard ad meets the Truth in Lending advertising rules. So we're fine, right?
Technical compliance with TILA doesn't insulate the rest of the ad. The CFPB procedures say that directly.
And our complaints log has 40 calls this quarter about 'free' checking that wasn't free.
That's a reasonable-consumer signal. Examiners would read those complaints before they read our ad.

cards.title: The 'free checking' billboard
cards.situation: Tom's billboard says 'Free checking. Earn USD 300.' The account is free only with a monthly direct deposit or a minimum balance; the bonus needs 90 days and a set amount of deposits. Conditions are on the website only. Complaints about surprise monthly fees are rising. What do you recommend?

choices.text: Revise the ad so the key conditions sit next to the headline, review the complaint pattern, and brief branch and call staff on the exact conditions
choices.outcome: Best. It fixes the net impression, uses proximity and prominence, treats complaints as a signal, and makes sure staff describe the product accurately.

choices.text: Keep the ad because the conditions are on the website and TILA advertising rules are met
choices.outcome: Poor. Technical compliance with TILA does not protect an ad whose overall impression misleads. Website-only conditions are not near the claim.

choices.text: Add a tiny asterisk and 'conditions apply' in small print at the bottom
choices.outcome: Partly right. It acknowledges conditions, but small print may not cure a misleading headline, and the key conditions are still hidden.

choices.text: Tell the complaints team to explain the conditions to callers one by one
choices.outcome: Poor. It treats the symptom, not the cause, and leaves a likely deceptive ad running.

cards.title: UDAAP enforcement in numbers (CFPB)
cards.caption: Figures from the CFPB's own enforcement action pages.

items.label: Wells Fargo, 2022
items.detail: Over USD 2bn redress and a USD 1.7bn penalty for auto, mortgage and deposit practices.

items.label: Bank of America, 2023
items.detail: Approximate redress for repeat NSF fees, plus a USD 60m CFPB penalty.

items.label: TD Bank, 2020
items.detail: Estimated restitution over overdraft enrolment practices, plus a USD 25m penalty.

cards.title: Real case: repeat NSF fees at Bank of America, 2023
cards.body:
When a customer's check or ACH debit bounced, Bank of America charged a USD 35 non-sufficient funds (NSF) fee. Merchants often **re-present** the same item, sometimes the very next day. Until February 2022 the bank charged **another** NSF fee each time the same item was returned again.

The CFPB found this **unfair** under the Consumer Financial Protection Act. The order in July 2023 required the bank to refund about **USD 80.4 million** in repeat fees and pay a **USD 60 million** civil penalty. The OCC separately fined the bank USD 60 million.

**Lesson:** a fee can be disclosed and still be unfair. The harm was substantial in total, customers could not control when a merchant re-presented an item, and repeat fees for the same item offered no real benefit.

Source: CFPB enforcement action page, docket 2023-CFPB-0006.

cards.title: Real case: TD Bank overdraft enrolment, 2020
cards.body:
In August 2020 the CFPB issued a consent order against **TD Bank, N.A.** over its optional overdraft service for ATM and one-time debit card transactions.

The CFPB found that TD Bank:

- charged overdraft fees **without the customer's affirmative consent**, breaching the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E;
- made **misleading statements** about the service in branches, by phone and in mailings, which was **deceptive**;
- **materially interfered** with customers' ability to understand its terms, which was **abusive**.

The order required an estimated **USD 97 million** in restitution and a **USD 25 million** penalty.

**Lesson:** one sales script can breach a specific rule and all three UDAAP standards. Front-line training on exactly what to say, and what not to say, is a control.

Source: CFPB enforcement action page, docket 2020-BCFP-0007.

cards.front: Myth: if it's in the terms and conditions, it can't be deceptive.
cards.back: Fact: fine print or later disclosures may not cure a misleading headline or a prominent claim.
Fact: intent is not needed. A claim can be deceptive if it is likely to mislead a reasonable consumer.

cards.front: Myth: if most customers understand, it's fine.
cards.back: Fact: misleading a significant minority of the target audience can be enough.

cards.front: Myth: following TILA's ad rules makes an ad safe.
cards.back: Fact: an ad can meet TILA and still contain other statements that are deceptive.

cards.front: Myth: no complaints means no UDAAP problem.
cards.back: Fact: an absence of complaints does not prove compliance, but patterns of complaints are a strong warning.

cards.front: Myth: abusive is just another word for unfair.
cards.back: Fact: unfair, deceptive and abusive each have their own legal standard.

cards.question: A bank markets a high-cost credit product to recent immigrants. How should its compliance team judge whether the marketing is deceptive?
options: By how a reasonable member of that target group would understand it
By how a financial expert would read the full contract
By whether the product is profitable for the bank
By whether a competitor uses similar wording
cards.explanation: The CFPB procedures say that when marketing targets a specific audience, it must be judged from the view of a reasonable member of that group.

cards.title: UDAAP review in your daily work
cards.body:
Before something reaches customers, ask:

- **What will people believe** after a quick look? Is that true?
- **Is the key condition next to the claim**, as prominent as the headline?
- **Who is the audience**, and would a reasonable member of it understand?
- **Can customers avoid the fee or harm**, or is it out of their control?
- **What do complaints, refunds and chargebacks say?** High volumes are a signal examiners also use.

cards.title: Stage two take-aways
items: UDAAP is banned by the Dodd-Frank Act; unfair, deceptive and abusive each have separate tests.
Unfair: substantial injury, not reasonably avoidable, not outweighed by benefits.
Deceptive: likely to mislead, reasonable interpretation by the target audience, material.
Abusive: interfering with understanding or taking unreasonable advantage of a consumer.
Meeting a specific rule such as TILA does not make a misleading message safe.
Complaints, refunds and chargebacks are signals both you and examiners should read.

cards.prompt: Pick one product message you use with customers. Would a reasonable member of your least experienced customer group understand its key cost and conditions? What would you change?

quiz.question: Which law makes unfair, deceptive or abusive acts or practices unlawful for providers of consumer financial products?
options: The Bank Secrecy Act, as amended by the USA PATRIOT Act
The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, through its financial privacy subtitle
The Dodd-Frank Act (Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010)
The Truth in Savings Act, through its advertising rules
quiz.explanation: Title X of the Dodd-Frank Act, the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010, contains the UDAAP prohibition for covered persons and service providers.

quiz.question: Which is NOT one of the three elements of unfairness?
options: The injury is substantial
The injury is not reasonably avoidable
The bank intended to harm the consumer
The injury is not outweighed by benefits
quiz.explanation: Unfairness requires substantial injury, not reasonably avoidable, and not outweighed by benefits to consumers or competition. Intent is not an element.

quiz.question: A bank charges a fee each time a merchant re-presents the same returned ACH item. Which UDAAP standard did the CFPB apply to this practice at Bank of America in 2023?
options: Unfair
Abusive only
Deceptive only
None; it was found lawful
quiz.explanation: The CFPB found Bank of America's repeat NSF fees unfair under the Consumer Financial Protection Act and ordered refunds and a penalty.

quiz.question: Information about which of these is generally presumed material under the deception test?
options: The colour scheme of the bank's logo
The name of the branch manager
The font size used in a printed product brochure
A product's cost, benefits or restrictions
quiz.explanation: The CFPB procedures say information about the central features of a product, such as cost, benefits or restrictions, is presumed material.

quiz.question: An ad meets every Regulation Z advertising rule but also claims the loan has 'no hidden costs' when it does. What is the risk?
options: None, because Regulation Z compliance is a safe harbour
The extra claim can still be deceptive
Only a state law issue, not federal
Only a problem if a court has ruled on it
quiz.explanation: The CFPB procedures note that technical compliance with TILA does not insulate the rest of an ad from being deceptive.

quiz.question: Which description matches the abusive standard?
options: Taking unreasonable advantage of a consumer's lack of understanding
Any fee that is above the average for the local market
Any practice that at least one customer has complained about in writing
Any credit product that carries a variable interest rate
quiz.explanation: An abusive practice materially interferes with understanding of a term or takes unreasonable advantage of lack of understanding, inability to protect interests, or reasonable reliance.

quiz.question: Most customers understand a bonus offer, but a significant minority of the target audience is misled. What follows under the deception standard?
options: It is lawful because most understood
It is lawful if the bank meant well
The offer can still be deceptive
It is only deceptive if all are misled
quiz.explanation: The CFPB procedures say a representation may be deceptive if a significant minority of the target audience is misled, even if most consumers are not.

quiz.question: Which of the FTC's 'four Ps' asks whether a disclosure sits close to the claim it qualifies?
options: Prominence
Proximity
Placement
Presentation
quiz.explanation: Proximity asks whether the disclosure is near the claim it qualifies. Prominence is about noticeability, placement about where people look, presentation about clarity.

quiz.question: In the 2020 TD Bank case, which finding was based on Regulation E rather than UDAAP?
options: Making misleading statements about the service by phone
Interfering with customers' understanding of the terms
Sending misleading mailed solicitations to customers
Charging overdraft fees without affirmative consent
quiz.explanation: The CFPB found TD Bank charged overdraft fees on ATM and one-time debit card transactions without affirmative consent, violating EFTA and Regulation E. The misleading statements were deceptive and the interference was abusive.

quiz.question: Your team sees a sharp rise in refunds and chargebacks on a new add-on product, but few formal complaints. What is the best reading?
options: It proves the product is compliant and well liked
It only matters for the finance team's budgeting
It can be ignored until written complaints appear
It may signal a UDAAP problem worth reviewing
quiz.explanation: The CFPB procedures note that high volumes of refunds or chargebacks can indicate potential UDAAP issues, even if they do not appear in complaint records.

sessions.title: Regulation E: Electronic Fund Transfers and Error Resolution
sessions.summary: Handle electronic fund transfer disputes the way Regulation E requires: what counts as an error, oral notices, the 10-business-day clock, provisional credit, extended periods, results and liability limits.
objectives: Identify what is and is not an error under Regulation E
Apply the investigation timelines, including provisional credit and extended periods
Explain what the bank must tell the customer when it finds an error or no error
Describe consumer liability limits for unauthorised transfers and why automated tools cannot replace investigation

cards.title: The disputes queue
cards.setting: Card disputes centre, Denver, Colorado. 9:10 am.

lines.text: Morning. We have 340 open card disputes. Last week the fraud system flagged half of them as 'customer probably did it'.
Some of my team want to close those automatically. Faster queue, happier managers.
Regulation E doesn't let a fraud score replace an investigation. And the clock started the day each customer called.
Three of those callers have already complained to the CFPB. They say we told them to put it in writing first.
Then we may have a timing problem as well. Stage three: error resolution, step by step.

cards.title: Regulation E error resolution in five scenes

scenes.heading: What it covers
scenes.narration: Regulation E, issued by the CFPB under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, protects consumers who use debit cards, ATMs, online transfers and other electronic fund transfers from their accounts.

scenes.heading: What counts as an error
scenes.narration: Errors include unauthorised transfers, wrong amounts, transfers missing from a statement, bank bookkeeping mistakes, wrong cash from an ATM, and a request for documentation or clarification about a transfer.

scenes.heading: Oral notice counts
scenes.narration: A customer can give notice by phone. The bank may ask for written confirmation, but must start investigating right away and cannot wait for the letter.

scenes.heading: The clock
scenes.narration: The bank generally has 10 business days to decide. If it needs longer, it can take up to 45 days, but only if it provisionally credits the customer within those 10 business days.

scenes.heading: Closing the loop
scenes.narration: The bank reports results, explains in writing if it finds no error, offers the documents it relied on, and corrects real errors quickly.

cards.title: Regulation E: the key clocks
cards.caption: Periods from 12 CFR 1005.11 as published on consumerfinance.gov. New accounts have longer periods.

items.label: Customer's notice window
items.detail: From when the statement first showing the error is sent.

items.label: Investigate or provisionally credit
items.detail: Also the window for any written confirmation the bank asks for.

items.label: Tell the customer about the credit
items.detail: Amount and date; full use of the funds during the investigation.

items.label: Longest standard investigation
items.detail: Extended to 90 days for some transfers, such as point-of-sale debit card ones.

items.label: Report the results
items.detail: After the investigation ends; correct a real error within one business day.

cards.question: A customer calls on day one to dispute a debit card charge. The bank asks for written confirmation. When must the investigation start?
options: When the written confirmation arrives
Promptly, on receiving the oral notice
After 10 business days
Only once the merchant replies
cards.explanation: The official interpretation says the bank must begin investigating promptly on an oral notice and may not delay until written confirmation arrives. It may skip provisional credit only if it required written confirmation and did not get it within 10 business days.

cards.title: Provisional credit and the extended timelines
Work a Regulation E dispute in order
cards.prompt: Put the steps of a dispute that needs more than 10 business days in order.
steps: Receive the customer's notice of error, by phone or in writing
Start investigating straight away, without waiting for written confirmation
Provisionally credit the account within 10 business days
Tell the customer the amount and date of the credit within two business days
Finish the investigation within the allowed period
Report the results within three business days, with a written explanation if no error is found

cards.title: The fraud filter
cards.setting: Denver, the disputes team huddle. 11:30 am.

lines.text: Here's the proposal: if the fraud model scores a claim as 'likely first-party', we deny it and close the case.
That's very close to a real enforcement case. The CFPB found a bank relied solely on an automated filter and denied claims without reasonable investigation.
So the model is useless?
No. Use it to prioritise and guide. But a real investigation must look at the facts, and the customer must get the timelines and explanations Regulation E requires.

cards.title: Closing disputes on a fraud score
cards.situation: A customer reports three debit card transactions she says she did not make. The fraud model scores the claim 'likely customer-initiated'. It is day 8 after her phone call and the team has not looked at the transactions. A supervisor suggests denying the claim today to keep the queue down. What do you do?

choices.text: Investigate the facts now, and if you can't finish by day 10, provisionally credit her and tell her within two business days
choices.outcome: Best. A score can guide an investigation but not replace it. The 10-business-day clock is running, and provisional credit keeps the 45- or 90-day option open.

choices.text: Deny the claim today based on the score and send a standard letter
choices.outcome: Poor. Relying solely on a filter without a reasonable investigation is what the CFPB found unfair and in breach of Regulation E in the Bank of America case.

choices.text: Wait for her written statement before doing anything
choices.outcome: Poor. The bank may ask for written confirmation, but it cannot delay starting or completing the investigation while waiting.

choices.text: Credit her permanently without investigating to save time
choices.outcome: Partly right. A bank may correct without investigation in the amount alleged, and must still meet the other rules, but doing this routinely ignores fraud risk.

cards.title: Real case: Bank of America unemployment benefit cards, 2022
Error or not an error?
cards.prompt: Match each customer request to how Regulation E treats it.

pairs.right: An error: an unauthorised electronic fund transfer

pairs.left: 'The ATM gave me USD 60, not USD 100'
pairs.right: An error: receiving the wrong amount from an electronic terminal
Not an error: a routine balance inquiry

pairs.left: 'Can you send me a copy for my taxes?'
pairs.right: Not an error: a request for tax or record-keeping information

pairs.left: 'Please explain this transfer on my statement'
pairs.right: An error notice: a request for clarification about a transfer

cards.title: Consumer liability for unauthorised transfers
cards.caption: Summary of 12 CFR 1005.6(b) in our own words. The bank applies the detailed rule.

items.label: Lost or stolen card, reported within two business days
items.left: Lesser of USD 50 or the transfers before notice
items.right: Report fast to keep liability lowest

items.label: Reported later than two business days
items.left: Up to USD 500, subject to the rule's conditions
items.right: Bank must show later losses were avoidable

items.label: Unauthorised transfer on a statement, not reported within 60 days
items.left: May be liable for later transfers the bank shows were avoidable
items.right: Staff should urge customers to check statements

items.label: Extenuating circumstances, such as hospital stay
items.left: Time limits extended to a reasonable period

cards.front: Can the customer's notice be oral?
cards.back: Yes. A phone call is a valid notice of error. The bank can ask for written confirmation within 10 business days.

cards.front: Must the notice include the account number?
cards.back: No, if the bank can identify the account another way, the notice is still effective.

cards.front: Can the bank charge for investigating?
cards.back: No charge if an error occurred. The commentary warns against charges that would chill good-faith claims.

cards.front: What if the bank finds no error?
cards.back: It explains its findings in writing and tells the customer they can ask for the documents it relied on.

cards.front: What if it reverses a provisional credit?
cards.back: It notifies the customer and honours cheques and preauthorised transfers for five business days without overdraft charges, as the rule sets out.

cards.front: Does closing the account end the right?
cards.back: No. A properly asserted error must be handled even if the account is closed.

cards.question: A bank investigated a dispute, found no error and reversed the provisional credit. Which step does Regulation E require?
options: Close the account to prevent repeat claims
Charge a research fee for the investigation
Explain the finding in writing and offer the documents relied on
Report the customer to a consumer reporting agency
cards.explanation: When the bank finds no error, its report must include a written explanation and note the customer's right to request the documents it relied on. It must also give notice of the debit and honour items for five business days.

cards.title: Real case: Wells Fargo account freezes, 2022
cards.body:
The CFPB's December 2022 order against **Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.** covered auto loans, mortgages and deposit accounts. On deposits, the CFPB found the bank **unfairly froze consumer accounts when fraud was suspected** even though lesser restraints were available. It also found deceptive claims about monthly fee waivers and unfair overdraft fees charged when customers had enough available funds at the time of the transaction.

The order required more than **USD 2 billion** in redress and a **USD 1.7 billion** penalty.

**Lesson for disputes and fraud teams:** fraud controls protect the bank and its customers, but blunt tools such as freezing a whole account can themselves harm consumers. Choose the least harmful control that does the job, document why, and keep error resolution moving.

Source: CFPB enforcement action page, docket 2022-CFPB-0011.

cards.title: Stage three take-aways
items: Regulation E errors include unauthorised transfers, wrong amounts, omissions, bank mistakes and requests for clarification.
Oral notice counts; investigation starts at once and cannot wait for written confirmation.
Decide within 10 business days, or provisionally credit and take up to 45 days (90 in set cases).
Report results within three business days; if no error, explain in writing and offer the documents.
Automated fraud tools can guide but cannot replace a reasonable investigation.

cards.prompt: If you handle or route customer disputes, where could a Regulation E clock be lost today: at the first call, in a handoff, or waiting for paperwork? Who would you tell?

quiz.question: Within how many business days must a bank generally determine whether an error occurred under Regulation E, unless it provisionally credits the account?
options: 5 business days
30 business days
60 business days
10 business days
quiz.explanation: 12 CFR 1005.11(c)(1) gives 10 business days to determine whether an error occurred. With provisional credit, the bank may take up to 45 days.

quiz.question: Which of these is an 'error' under Regulation E?
options: A routine question about the current account balance
An ATM dispensing less cash than the customer requested
A request for a duplicate statement for tax purposes
A question about the local branch's weekend opening hours
quiz.explanation: Receiving an incorrect amount of money from an electronic terminal is listed as an error. Balance inquiries and duplicate copies for tax purposes are excluded.

quiz.question: A customer gives oral notice of an error. The bank requires written confirmation and tells the customer where to send it. The letter never arrives. What does the bank NOT have to do?
options: Provisionally credit the account
Investigate the alleged error
Report the result to the customer
Correct any error it does find
quiz.explanation: If the bank requires written confirmation and does not receive it within 10 business days, it need not provisionally credit. It must still investigate and resolve the notice.

quiz.question: After provisionally crediting an account, how soon must the bank tell the customer the amount and date of the credit?
options: Within 10 business days
Within 30 days
Within two business days
At the next periodic statement
quiz.explanation: 1005.11(c)(2)(ii) requires the bank to inform the consumer within two business days after the provisional crediting.

quiz.question: A customer disputes a point-of-sale debit card transaction. With provisional credit made in time, what is the maximum period to complete the investigation?
options: 45 days
90 days
60 days
120 days
quiz.explanation: The 45-day period becomes 90 days for transfers resulting from point-of-sale debit card transactions, transfers not initiated within a state, and new-account transfers.

quiz.question: After finishing an investigation, how quickly must the bank report the results to the customer?
options: Within one business day
Within 10 business days
Within 60 calendar days of notice
Within three business days
quiz.explanation: The bank must report results within three business days after completing the investigation, and correct a real error within one business day of determining it.

quiz.question: In the 2022 Bank of America prepaid card case, what practice did the CFPB find unfair?
options: Paying unemployment benefits to cardholders faster than the states required
Offering prepaid debit cards to people receiving government benefits
Using any kind of automated fraud detection at all on its prepaid card accounts
Denying error claims and freezing accounts based solely on a flawed fraud filter
quiz.explanation: The CFPB found the bank relied solely on an automated fraud filter it knew or should have known was flawed to deny claims and freeze accounts.

quiz.question: A customer reports their lost debit card within two business days of learning it was lost. What is their maximum liability for unauthorised transfers?
options: Nothing at all, in every case
The lesser of USD 50 or the transfers before notice
USD 500 in all cases, regardless of timing
The full amount of every unauthorised transfer made
quiz.explanation: Under 1005.6(b)(1), timely notice caps liability at the lesser of USD 50 or the amount of unauthorised transfers before notice.

quiz.question: An investigation finds no error. What must the bank's report include?
options: Only an oral statement of the result, given at the branch or by phone
A fee for the investigation, deducted from the account balance
A written explanation and notice of the right to see the documents relied on
A notice that the account will be closed to prevent the customer making further claims
quiz.explanation: 1005.11(d)(1) requires a written explanation of the findings and notice of the right to request the documents the bank relied on.

quiz.question: A customer's account was closed last month. She now properly asserts an error on a transfer from before closure. What applies?
options: The error resolution procedures still apply
Nothing, because closed accounts are out of scope
Only state law applies once an account is closed
She must reopen the account before she can dispute
quiz.explanation: The official interpretation says the bank must comply with error resolution when an error is properly asserted, even if the account is closed.

sessions.title: Credit: Regulation Z, Loan Originator Rules and ECOA/Regulation B
sessions.summary: Learn the Truth in Lending disclosure clocks for mortgages, the loan originator screening and training rule, and the equal credit rules in Regulation B, including the 2026 removal of the effects test.
objectives: Apply the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure timing rules
Explain the screening, fitness and periodic training duties for loan originator employees
Identify prohibited bases, discouragement and adverse action notice duties under Regulation B
Describe what the April 2026 Regulation B amendment changed and what it did not

lines.text: Good news: we hired Daniel, an experienced loan officer from a credit union. He starts taking applications Monday.
Before Monday, did we run the NMLS background check, pull his credit report and make the fitness decision? And is his periodic training booked?
He's registered in NMLS already. Isn't that enough?
Registration is one piece. Regulation Z puts its own duties on us as his employer, including training on federal and state law.
And the new Regulation B changes from July. My team keeps asking whether fair lending still matters.
It absolutely does. Stage four: Truth in Lending, loan originator rules, and equal credit.

cards.title: Truth in Lending and equal credit in five scenes

scenes.heading: TILA and Regulation Z
scenes.narration: The Truth in Lending Act, put into effect by the CFPB's Regulation Z, makes lenders disclose the cost of credit clearly, such as the annual percentage rate and the finance charge, so consumers can compare offers.

scenes.heading: Mortgage disclosures
scenes.narration: For most closed-end mortgages, the Loan Estimate goes out within three business days of application, and the consumer must receive the Closing Disclosure at least three business days before closing.

scenes.heading: Loan originators
scenes.narration: Banks that employ mortgage loan originators must screen them before they originate and give them periodic training on the federal and state law that applies to their work.

scenes.heading: Equal credit
scenes.narration: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act and Regulation B ban discrimination on a prohibited basis in any part of a credit transaction, for every creditor.

scenes.heading: The 2026 change
scenes.narration: In April 2026 the CFPB amended Regulation B to remove the disparate-impact 'effects test', effective 21 July 2026. Intentional and different treatment on a prohibited basis is still illegal.

cards.title: Mortgage disclosure clocks (Regulation Z)
cards.caption: From 12 CFR 1026.19(e) and (f) on consumerfinance.gov. Timeshare transactions and some waivers follow special rules.

items.label: Loan Estimate after application
items.detail: Delivered or mailed no later than the third business day after the application.

items.label: Before consummation
items.detail: Loan Estimate delivered or mailed at least seven business days before closing.

items.label: Closing Disclosure received
items.detail: Consumer must receive it at least three business days before consummation.

cards.question: A loan officer wants to collect an application fee before the consumer has received the Loan Estimate. What does Regulation Z say?
options: Allowed if the fee is small
Allowed if disclosed verbally
Generally not allowed until the consumer gets the Loan Estimate and says they want to proceed
Allowed only for first-time buyers
cards.explanation: Under 1026.19(e)(2), apart from a narrow exception for a credit report fee, no fee may be imposed before the consumer has received the Loan Estimate and indicated an intent to proceed.

cards.title: The loan originator training rule: 12 CFR 1026.36(f)
cards.body:
Regulation Z sets **qualification duties** for employers of mortgage loan originators. For each loan originator employee who is **not required to be licensed** (typical for bank staff, who register in the Nationwide Mortgage Licensing System and Registry, NMLSR), the bank must:

- **Before** the person originates (for hires on or after 1 January 2014, or where reliable information raises doubts): get an **NMLSR criminal background check**, a **credit report**, and NMLSR information on any administrative, civil or criminal findings.
- **Decide** the person meets the standards: broadly, no felony in the past **seven years**, or ever for felonies involving fraud, dishonesty, breach of trust or money laundering (unless a consent applies), and financial responsibility, character and general fitness.
- Provide **periodic training** covering the federal and state law requirements that apply to the person's origination work: 1026.36(f)(3)(iii).

The loan documents must also show the organisation's and the originator's names and NMLSR IDs (1026.36(g)).

cards.title: Allowed or not under ECOA and Regulation B?

items.text: Declining an applicant because of their religion
Considering verified income and debts to judge repayment ability
Treating income from a public assistance programme as worthless
Using age as a variable in a sound, validated scoring system without penalising older applicants
Advertising that suggests applicants of one national origin should not apply
Sending an adverse action notice with the specific reasons for denial
Refusing credit because a customer once disputed a bill under consumer credit law

cards.title: Does fair lending still matter?
cards.setting: Mortgage centre team meeting, Phoenix. 3:00 pm.

lines.text: My loan officers read headlines saying 'disparate impact is gone'. Some think fair lending checks are now optional.
The April 2026 rule says ECOA doesn't recognise the effects test, effective 21 July 2026. That's a real change in Regulation B.
But treating applicants differently on a prohibited basis, or discouraging them, is still illegal. Most enforcement cases were about exactly that.
So our scripts and ads still need review?
Yes. And other federal and state laws can have their own fair lending rules, so we check with legal before we change anything.

cards.title: The 'neighbourhood' comment
cards.situation: A customer of Middle Eastern origin asks a loan officer about a home equity loan. The officer says, 'Honestly, people from your community usually don't get approved here, you might try somewhere else.' The customer leaves without applying. The officer says nothing was denied, so no rule applies. What should happen?

choices.text: Escalate to compliance as possible discouragement on a prohibited basis, review the officer's other files, and retrain
choices.outcome: Best. Regulation B bans statements a creditor knows or should know would make a reasonable person think they'd be denied because of a prohibited basis, such as national origin. No application is needed.

choices.text: Do nothing because no application was taken and no credit was denied
choices.outcome: Poor. Discouragement covers prospective applicants. A statement like this is a fair lending concern even without an application.

choices.text: Ask the officer to apologise if the customer comes back
choices.outcome: Partly right. An apology may help, but it does not deal with the compliance risk, other affected customers or training.

choices.text: Treat it as an HR matter only, since the April 2026 rule removed disparate impact
choices.outcome: Poor. The 2026 change concerns the effects test. A statement aimed at national origin is about intent and treatment, which is still prohibited.

cards.title: Regulation B: what changed in 2026 and what did not

items.label: Disparate impact ('effects test')
items.left: Removed from Regulation B; ECOA stated not to recognise it

items.label: Discrimination on a prohibited basis
items.left: Still prohibited in any aspect of a credit transaction

items.label: Discouragement
items.left: Now focused on statements showing intent, judged by a reasonable person
items.right: Scripts and ads still need review

items.label: Special purpose credit programmes
items.left: Race, colour, national origin or sex can't be the shared characteristic

items.label: Adverse action notices
items.left: Unchanged: notify within 30 days with specific reasons or the right to them

cards.title: Real case: Citibank and Armenian American applicants, 2023
cards.body:
In November 2023 the CFPB issued an order against **Citibank, N.A.** finding that it violated ECOA and Regulation B by **discriminating against certain credit card applicants based on national origin**. The CFPB also found Citibank failed to give accurate and adequate statements of the **specific reasons** for adverse action when applicants were denied on that basis.

The order required **USD 1.4 million** in redress and a **USD 24.5 million** civil money penalty.

In October 2025 the CFPB **terminated** the order early, noting Citibank had paid the penalty, made redress and taken steps to prevent future violations.

**Lesson:** this was intentional, different treatment, the kind of conduct the 2026 Regulation B change did not touch. Adverse action reasons must be the real reasons.

Source: CFPB enforcement action page, docket 2023-CFPB-0013.

cards.title: Real case: Trustmark National Bank, 2021
cards.body:
In October 2021 the CFPB and the US Department of Justice filed a joint complaint alleging that **Trustmark National Bank** violated ECOA, Regulation B and the Consumer Financial Protection Act. The agencies' press release described it as deliberate discrimination against Black and Hispanic families in mortgage lending. The OCC took part in the announcement.

A federal court in Tennessee entered a consent order with injunctive relief and a civil money penalty.

In **May 2025**, on the agencies' unopposed motion, the court **vacated** the 2021 judgment and dismissed the case.

**Lesson:** enforcement priorities change, and orders can end early. The underlying ban on discrimination in ECOA did not change. Your bank's fair lending programme should not rise and fall with headlines.

Source: CFPB enforcement action page, docket 2:21-cv-02664.

cards.title: Match the rule to its requirement
cards.prompt: Link each Regulation Z or B provision to what it requires.

pairs.right: Loan Estimate within three business days after application
Closing Disclosure received three business days before consummation
Periodic training for loan originator employees on federal and state law
Names and NMLSR IDs on application, disclosures, note and security instrument
Notice of action taken, generally within 30 days, with reasons or the right to them
No statements that would discourage applicants on a prohibited basis

cards.back: Annual percentage rate: the cost of credit as a yearly rate, a core TILA disclosure.
The cost of consumer credit as a dollar amount, disclosed under TILA.
Nationwide Mortgage Licensing System and Registry. Bank loan originators register there and get an NMLSR ID.
Race, colour, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age (with capacity to contract), public assistance income, or good-faith exercise of consumer credit rights.
A denial, unfavourable change or refusal of credit on the terms requested, which triggers a notice.
The disparate-impact theory that a neutral policy can be illegal because of its outcomes. Removed from Regulation B from 21 July 2026.

cards.question: Which applicant characteristic is a prohibited basis under Regulation B?
options: The applicant's credit history
The applicant's debt-to-income ratio
The applicant's employment length
The fact that income comes from a public assistance programme
cards.explanation: Regulation B lists the fact that all or part of income comes from public assistance as a prohibited basis. Credit history, debt and job tenure are legitimate credit factors when used consistently.

cards.title: Stage four take-aways
items: TILA and Regulation Z require clear credit cost disclosures; mortgage Loan Estimates and Closing Disclosures have strict timing.
Banks must screen loan originator employees before they originate and give them periodic training: 12 CFR 1026.36(f)(3).
ECOA and Regulation B ban discrimination on a prohibited basis and discouragement of applicants.
From 21 July 2026 Regulation B no longer uses the disparate-impact effects test; intentional discrimination is still illegal.
Adverse action notices must give the real, specific reasons or the right to get them.

cards.prompt: If you talk to credit applicants, think of one phrase you use when someone probably won't qualify. Could a reasonable person hear it as being about who they are rather than their finances?

quiz.question: Under Regulation Z, by when must a creditor deliver or mail the Loan Estimate for a covered mortgage?
options: By the third business day after receiving the application
No later than the day of closing, with the other documents
Within 30 calendar days of receiving the application
Only if the consumer asks for an estimate in writing
quiz.explanation: 1026.19(e)(1)(iii)(A) requires delivery or mailing no later than the third business day after the creditor receives the application.

quiz.question: When must the consumer receive the Closing Disclosure for a typical covered mortgage?
options: At closing, along with the note
Seven business days after closing
At least three business days before consummation
Within 60 days of receiving the application
quiz.explanation: 1026.19(f)(1)(ii)(A) requires the consumer to receive the Closing Disclosure no later than three business days before consummation, with special cases such as timeshares.

quiz.question: Which Regulation Z provision requires periodic training for a bank's loan originator employees?
quiz.explanation: 1026.36(f)(3)(iii) requires periodic training covering federal and state law requirements that apply to the individual's loan origination activities.

quiz.question: What must the periodic loan originator training cover?
options: Only the bank's own sales targets and product features
Only federal anti-money laundering and sanctions rules
Only the bank's loan origination IT systems and how to use their screens
Federal and state law that applies to the person's origination work
quiz.explanation: The rule requires training on the federal and state law requirements that apply to the individual loan originator's origination activities.

quiz.question: Before a newly hired bank loan originator takes applications, which check does 1026.36(f)(3) require?
options: A polygraph test arranged by the bank
A home visit by a senior manager
A personal reference from a current customer and a former employer
An NMLSR criminal background check and a credit report
quiz.explanation: The bank must obtain a criminal background check through NMLSR, a credit report and NMLSR information on findings, then decide whether the person meets the standards.

quiz.question: Which is a prohibited basis under Regulation B?
options: Credit score
Marital status
Monthly income
Existing debt
quiz.explanation: Prohibited bases include race, colour, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age (with capacity to contract), public assistance income and good-faith exercise of consumer credit rights.

quiz.question: What did the CFPB's April 2026 amendment to Regulation B do?
options: Repealed the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and Regulation B entirely
Removed the ban on intentional discrimination on a prohibited basis
Removed the disparate-impact effects test, effective 21 July 2026
Abolished adverse action notices for consumer credit applications
quiz.explanation: The rule removed the effects test and stated ECOA does not recognise disparate impact liability; it also changed discouragement and special purpose credit programmes. Intentional discrimination remains prohibited.

quiz.question: A creditor denies a completed credit application. Generally, within how many days must it notify the applicant?
options: 30 days
10 days
60 days
90 days
quiz.explanation: 1002.9(a)(1)(i) requires notice of action taken within 30 days after receiving a completed application. 90 days applies to unaccepted counteroffers.

quiz.question: A loan officer tells a walk-in visitor, 'People of your faith don't usually qualify here.' No application is taken. Which statement is correct?
options: No rule applies because no application was taken
This can be prohibited discouragement even without an application
It is allowed after the 2026 Regulation B amendment
It is only a matter of customer service politeness, not legal compliance
quiz.explanation: Regulation B's discouragement rule covers statements to prospective applicants that a reasonable person would take as meaning they'd be denied because of a prohibited basis such as religion.

quiz.question: In the 2023 Citibank case, what did the CFPB find in addition to national origin discrimination?
options: Late Closing Disclosures on mortgage loans
Unlicensed loan originators taking applications
Missing annual privacy notices to its credit card holders nationwide
Failure to give accurate specific reasons for adverse action
quiz.explanation: The CFPB found Citibank failed to give accurate and adequate statements of specific reasons for adverse action to applicants denied based on national origin.

sessions.title: Complaints, Privacy, Collections and Exam Readiness
sessions.summary: Handle complaints the way examiners expect, apply Regulation P privacy notice and opt-out rules, see where Regulation F reaches collections, and assemble the evidence of a working compliance management system.
objectives: Run a complaint process that records, escalates, analyses and fixes
Apply Regulation P initial notice, annual notice and opt-out basics
Explain when Regulation F covers a bank's collections and where UDAAP still applies
Assemble exam-ready evidence across all parts of the compliance management system

cards.title: Complaints, privacy and the final week

lines.text: Welcome to Atlanta. This screen shows every complaint: branch, phone, email, social media, and the ones the CFPB forwards to us.
The CFPB portal ones have a clock. Companies generally respond in 15 days, and if we need longer we say it's in progress and finish within 60.
My partner team wants to share customer lists with an insurance company for a joint offer. Is that a privacy issue?
And our collections vendor asked if they can call as 'Lantern Recovery Services' instead of our name.
Three good questions for the last stage: complaints, privacy and collections. Then we put the whole CMS on the examiner's table.

cards.title: Complaints, privacy and collections in five scenes

scenes.heading: Every channel counts
scenes.narration: Examiners expect complaints from every channel to be recorded and categorised, whether they come by phone, letter, branch, social media or from a regulator.

scenes.heading: Escalate what matters
scenes.narration: Complaints that suggest discrimination, unauthorised accounts, improper sales, imminent foreclosure or other legal issues must be escalated, not just closed.

scenes.heading: Fix the cause
scenes.narration: Management uses complaints to find root causes and takes corrective action, including putting things right for customers already harmed.

scenes.heading: Privacy under Regulation P
scenes.narration: Banks give customers a privacy notice, generally every year, and let consumers opt out before sharing their nonpublic personal information with unaffiliated third parties, unless an exception applies.

scenes.heading: Debt collection
scenes.narration: Regulation F covers debt collectors, such as firms collecting debts owed to others. A bank collecting its own debts under another name can also count as a debt collector.

items.label: Capture
items.detail: Log complaints from every channel, including about service providers.

items.label: Categorise
items.detail: Tag the product, issue and any legal or regulatory risk.

items.label: Investigate and respond
items.detail: Make a good-faith effort to resolve each complaint promptly.

items.label: Escalate
items.detail: Send legal and harm issues to compliance and management.

items.label: Analyse root cause
items.detail: Look for patterns across complaints, refunds and chargebacks.

items.label: Correct and remediate
items.detail: Fix processes and training; put harmed customers right.

cards.question: A customer posts on social media that the bank opened a credit card she never applied for. How should the complaints team treat it?
options: Ignore it, because social media is not an official channel
Record it, categorise it as possible unauthorised account opening and escalate
Reply publicly with her account details to show the card was valid
Wait to see if she files a formal written complaint
cards.explanation: The CFPB manual expects complaints from any channel to be recorded and categorised, and those alleging unauthorised account openings to be escalated. Never share account details publicly.

cards.title: Regulation P privacy basics
cards.body:
Regulation P (12 CFR Part 1016) implements the privacy part of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act.

- **Initial notice.** Give a clear privacy notice to a new **customer** no later than when the customer relationship starts, for example when they open a deposit account or get a loan.
- **Annual notice.** Give customers a notice at least once in any 12 consecutive months, **unless** the bank shares only under the rule's exceptions and has not changed its sharing practices since the last notice.
- **Opt-out.** Before sharing a consumer's nonpublic personal information with a **nonaffiliated third party** outside the exceptions, the bank must give the initial and opt-out notices, a **reasonable opportunity** to opt out (the rule's mail example is 30 days), and respect an opt-out.
- **Consumers vs customers.** A one-off consumer, such as someone buying a cashier's cheque, has fewer notice rights than a customer with a continuing relationship.

Information security and breach response are separate duties covered in other training.

cards.title: Which rule is at stake?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation by the rule it mainly engages.

items.text: A CFPB portal complaint needs a response
Sharing customer lists with an unaffiliated insurer
A vendor calls about debts the bank owns
Annual privacy notice when sharing practices change
Many callers report the same surprise fee
The bank collects its own loans under a different trade name
A customer opts out of third-party sharing by phone
A branch complaint alleging unfair treatment by age

cards.title: The joint offer
cards.setting: Product team room, Kansas City, by video. 1:00 pm.

lines.text: The insurer is not our affiliate. They want names, addresses and account types for a marketing mail-out.
That's nonpublic personal information going to a nonaffiliated third party. Unless an exception applies, customers need notice and a real chance to opt out first.
Our notice says we don't share with third parties for marketing. So we'd be changing our practice?
Exactly. If we change, we tell customers before we share, give them time to opt out, and update our annual notice approach. Legal decides which exception, if any, fits.

cards.title: The collections script
cards.situation: Prairie Lantern Bank wants to use a vendor to call customers who are behind on credit card payments the bank still owns. The vendor suggests calling as 'Lantern Recovery Services', a name customers wouldn't link to the bank, and using a firm script stressing 'legal consequences'. Complaints about harsh calls are already rising. What do you recommend?

choices.text: Ask legal to review Regulation F before using another name, check the script for UDAAP risk, train and monitor the vendor, and track complaints
choices.outcome: Best. A creditor collecting its own debts under a name suggesting a third party can fall within Regulation F, and harsh or misleading scripts are a UDAAP risk regardless. Vendor oversight stays with the bank.

choices.text: Approve it, because Regulation F never applies to banks
choices.outcome: Poor. Regulation F's definition of debt collector includes a creditor that uses another name suggesting a third party is collecting.

choices.text: Keep the bank's name but let the vendor write its own script without review
choices.outcome: Partly right. Using the bank's own name helps, but unreviewed scripts and no monitoring leave UDAAP and vendor risk with the bank.

choices.text: Stop collecting overdue debts entirely
choices.outcome: Poor. Collection is lawful; the goal is lawful, fair collection, not abandoning it.

items.label: Isolated, high harm
items.detail: One complaint about discrimination or an unauthorised account: escalate now.

items.label: Widespread, high harm
items.detail: Pattern of surprise fees or wrongful freezes: escalate, fix, remediate.

items.label: Isolated, low harm
items.detail: A one-off service delay: resolve and record.

items.label: Widespread, low harm
items.detail: Many small irritations: analyse root cause and fix the process.

cards.title: Real case: Regions Bank surprise overdraft fees, 2022
cards.body:
In September 2022 the CFPB issued an order against **Regions Bank**, headquartered in Birmingham, Alabama, over what the CFPB's press release called illegal **surprise overdraft fees**, with a headline total of **USD 191 million**. The order included a **USD 50 million** civil money penalty and a redress plan.

In **July 2025** the CFPB **terminated** the order, noting that Regions had paid the penalty and made redress payments.

**Lessons for your CMS:**

- Fee practices that surprise customers show up first in **complaints**. Patterns should reach management fast.
- **Remediation** of past harm is part of what examiners and enforcers expect, not only fixing the future.
- Supervisory priorities shift, and orders can end early, but the underlying laws and private claims remain.

Source: CFPB enforcement action page, docket 2022-CFPB-0008.

cards.title: Real case: Bank of America garnishment processing, 2022
cards.body:
